nodes.name: Diffusion model for the latent log price process
nodes.statement: The following diffusion processes are commonly used to model financial asset price processes: \begin{equation} d\bX_t = \bmu_tdt + \bTheta_td\bW_t, \hspace{1cm} t\in [0,1], \end{equation} where $(\bmu_t) = (\mu_t^{(1)},\cdots,\mu_t^{(p)})^\mathrm{T}$ is a $p$-dimensional drift process, $(\bTheta_t)$ is a $p\times p$ matrix, the so-called covolatility process at time $t$, and $(\bW_t)$ is a $p$-dimensional standard Brownian motion.
nodes.statement_short: Itô diffusion $d\bX_t=\bmu_t dt+\bTheta_t d\bW_t$ on $[0,1]$ modelling $p$ latent log prices.

nodes.name: Integrated covariance (ICV) matrix
nodes.statement: The integrated covariance (ICV) matrix given by \begin{equation} \ICV :=\int_0^1 \bTheta_t\bTheta_t^\mathrm{T} dt \end{equation} is of fundamental importance in risk management and portfolio allocation for high-frequency financial data. In the one-dimensional case, the ICV matrix reduces to the integrated volatility.
nodes.statement_short: The ICV is the time-integral of $\bTheta_t\bTheta_t^{\mathrm{T}}$ over one trading day; in dimension one it is the integrated volatility.

nodes.name: Realized covariance (RCV) matrix
nodes.statement: The classical estimator of the ICV matrix is the so-called realized covariance (RCV) matrix, which is defined as follows. Suppose that we can observe the log price processes $\{X_{t_i}^{(j)}\}_{j=1}^p$ synchronously at recording time $t_i = i/n$, $i=0,1,\cdots,n$, during one trading day. Then the RCV matrix is defined as \[\RCV := \sum_{i=1}^n\Delta\bX_i(\Delta\bX_i)^{\mathrm{T}},\] where \[ \Delta\bX_i = \begin{pmatrix} \Delta X_i^{(1)}\\ \vdots \\ \Delta X_i^{(p)}\\ \end{pmatrix} = \begin{pmatrix} X_{t_i}^{(1)} - X_{t_{i-1}}^{(1)}\\ \vdots\\ X_{t_i}^{(p)} - X_{t_{i-1}}^{(p)} \end{pmatrix}. \]
nodes.statement_short: The classical ICV estimator: the sum of outer products of the synchronously observed log-price increments.
nodes.origin_citation: classical realized covariance; Andersen and Bollerslev 1998, Barndorff-Nielsen and Shephard 2002

nodes.name: Class $\mathcal{C}$ of diffusion processes
nodes.statement: Suppose that $(\bX_t)$ is a $p$-dimensional process satisfying (\ref{eq: Model}) and $\bTheta_t$ is c\`{a}dl\`{a}g. Then $(\bX_t)$ belongs to class $\mathcal{C}$ if, almost surely, there exist $\gamma_t\in D([0,1]; \mathbb{R})$ and $\bLambda$ a $p\times p$ matrix satisfying $\begin{rm}tr\end{rm}(\bLambda\bLambda^\mathrm{T}) = p$ such that \begin{equation} \bm\Theta_t = \gamma_t \bm \Lambda, \end{equation} where $D([0,1]; \mathbb{R})$ is the space of c\`{a}dl\`{a}g functions from $[0,1]$ to $\mathbb{R}$.
nodes.statement_short: A process is in class $\mathcal{C}$ when its covolatility factorizes as a scalar càdlàg process times a fixed matrix $\bLambda$ with $\mathrm{tr}(\bLambda\bLambda^{\mathrm{T}})=p$.
nodes.genus: $p$-dimensional process satisfying (\ref{eq: Model}) and $\bTheta_t$ is c\`{a}dl\`{a}g
differentia: there exist $\gamma_t\in D([0,1]; \mathbb{R})$ and $\bLambda$ a $p\times p$ matrix satisfying $\begin{rm}tr\end{rm}(\bLambda\bLambda^\mathrm{T}) = p$

nodes.name: Time-variation adjusted realized covariance (TVA) matrix
nodes.statement: Hence, an alternative estimator has been proposed, the time-variation adjusted realized covariance (TVA) matrix, which is defined as \[ \TVA:= \frac{\tr(\RCV)}{n}\sum_{i=1}^n \frac{\Delta\bX_i(\Delta\bX_i)^{\mT}}{|\Delta\bX_i|^2}.\] The basic idea is to eliminate the influence of the (unknown) covolatility process $(\gamma_t)$ from the limiting spectral relationship between the ICV matrix and its estimator TVA matrix.
nodes.statement_short: The TVA matrix self-normalizes each increment and rescales by $\mathrm{tr}(\RCV)/n$, removing the unknown covolatility level $(\gamma_t)$.

nodes.name: Simplest illustration of the effect of multiple transactions
nodes.statement: The effect of multiple transactions can be easily illustrated in the simplest case as follows. We set the number of stocks to $p=100$, the observation frequency to $n=390$ (one record per minute), and assume equally spaced observation times ($t_i=i/n$) and an equal number of transactions at each time point, i.e., $L_i\equiv L$, $i=1,2,\cdots,n$. Suppose that the log price processes $\{\bX_{s_j} \}$ are generated from the model $d\bX_s = \bLambda d\bW_s$, with $\bLambda=(0.5^{|k-\ell|})_{k,\ell=1,\cdots,p}$ and equally spaced time points $s_j=j/(nL)$, for $j=1,\cdots,nL$. The observations $\bX_{t_i}$ are approximated by the averages of $L$ multiple transaction prices at each time point $t_i$, that is, for $i=1,2,\cdots,n$, $ \bX_{t_i} = (1/L) \sum_{\ell=1}^L \bX_{s_{(i-1)L + \ell}}. $
nodes.statement_short: A $p=100$, $n=390$ simulation in which each recording time averages $L$ latent prices, used to show that the ESD of the TVA matrix moves with $L$.

nodes.name: Empirical spectral distribution (ESD)
nodes.statement: From random matrix theory, for any $p$-dimensional symmetric matrix $\bA$, the empirical spectral distribution (ESD) is defined as \begin{eqnarray} F^{\bA} (x) = \dfrac 1p \sum_{j=1}^p \ \indic (\lambda_j(\bA) \le x), ~~~~ \forall x\in \mathbb{R}, \end{eqnarray} where $\indic(\cdot)$ is an indicator function and $\lambda_j(\bA)$ denotes the $j$th largest eigenvalue of matrix $\bA$.

nodes.name: Limiting spectral distribution (LSD)
nodes.statement: The limit of ESD is referred to as the limiting spectral distribution (LSD), if it exists.

nodes.name: Stieltjes transform
nodes.statement: For any distribution function $F$, $m_F(\cdot)$ denotes its Stieltjes transform defined as \[m_F(z) = \int \frac{1}{\lambda - z}dF(\lambda), \hspace{1cm} \text{for~} z\in \mathbb{C}^+ :=\{z \in \mathbb{C}: \Im(z) > 0\},\] where $\Im(z)$ is the imaginary part of $z$

nodes.name: Average of multiple transaction prices $\ol{\bV}_i$
nodes.statement: One commonly used method to deal with multiple transactions involves taking averages of the multiple transaction prices at each time point $t_i$, that is, \[ \ol{\bV}_i = \dfrac{1}{L_i} \sum_{j=1}^{L_i} \bV_{T_{i-1}+j}, ~~~~~ i=1,\cdots,n, \] and using $\ol{\bV}_i$ to approximate the observation at time point $t_i$.
nodes.statement_short: Replace the $L_i$ prices recorded at $t_i$ by their arithmetic mean $\ol{\bV}_i$.
nodes.definiendum: $\ol{\bV}_i$, the average of multiple observations at recording time $t_i$

nodes.name: Asymmetric triangular decomposition of the averaged increment
nodes.statement_short: The averaged increment $\Delta\wbV_i$ rewrites as a weighted sum of tick increments with asymmetric triangular weights $a_{i,j},b_{i,j}$.

nodes.name: Non-overlapping averaged TVA (ATVA) matrix $\cA_N$
nodes.statement: To investigate the effect of multiple transactions, we start by studying the non-overlapping averaged TVA (ATVA) matrix, $\cA_N$, which is defined as \begin{equation} \cA_N := \dfrac{\sum_{i=1}^N |\Delta \ol{\bX}_{2i}|^2}{N} \cdot \sum_{i=1}^N \dfrac{\Delta\ol{\bX}_{2i} \Delta\ol{\bX}_{2i}^T}{|\Delta\ol{\bX}_{2i}|^2} = \dfrac{\sum_{i=1}^N |\Delta \ol{\bX}_{2i}|^2}{p} \cdot \wt{\bSigma}, \end{equation} where $N=\lfloor n/2 \rfloor$, $\wt{\bSigma}=\dfrac pN \sum_{i=1}^N \dfrac{\Delta\ol{\bX}_{2i} \Delta\ol{\bX}_{2i}^T}{|\Delta\ol{\bX}_{2i}|^2} $. Using the notation in \eqref{eqn:Delta_V}, the log return based on the averaged log prices becomes \[ \Delta\ol{\bX}_{2i} = \sum_{j=1}^{L_{2i}} a_{2i,j} \Delta_{2i,j} \bX + \sum_{j=1}^{L_{2i-1}}b_{2i-1,j} \Delta_{2i-1,j} \bX, \] where $\Delta_{i,j} \bX =\bX_{T_{i-1}+j} - \bX_{T_{i-1}+j-1}$.
nodes.statement_short: The ATVA matrix applies the TVA construction to non-overlapping even-indexed averaged log returns.
nodes.section: LSD of non-overlapping averaged TVA (ATVA) matrix

nodes.name: Assumption (A.i)
nodes.statement: For all $p$, $(\bX_t)$ is a $p$-dimensional process in class $\mathcal{C}$ for some drift process $\bmu_t = (\mu_t^{(1)},\cdots,\mu_t^{(p)})^{\mathrm{T}}$ and covolatility process $(\bTheta_t) = (\gamma_t\bLambda)$;
nodes.statement_short: The price process lies in class $\mathcal{C}$ with covolatility $\gamma_t\bLambda$.
nodes.section: LSD of non-overlapping averaged TVA (ATVA) matrix

nodes.name: Assumption (A.ii)
nodes.statement: there exists a $C_0<\infty$ such that for all $p$ and all $l = 1,\cdots,p$, $|\mu_t^{(l)}|\leq C_0$ for all $t\in[0,1)$ almost surely;
nodes.statement_short: The drift components are uniformly bounded.
nodes.section: LSD of non-overlapping averaged TVA (ATVA) matrix

nodes.name: Assumption (A.iii)
nodes.statement: there exists a $0\leq \delta_1<1/2$ and a sequence of index sets $\mathcal{I}_p$ satisfying $\mathcal{I}_p \subset \{1,\cdots, p\}$ and $\#\mathcal{I}_p = O(p^{\delta_1})$ such that $(\gamma_t)$ may depend on $\bW_t$ but only on $(W_t^{(l)}:l\in \mathcal{I}_p)$; moreover, there exists a $C_1<\infty$ such that for all $p$, $|\gamma_t|\in(1/C_1, C_1)$ for all $t\in [0,1)$, almost surely;
nodes.statement_short: $(\gamma_t)$ is bounded away from $0$ and $\infty$ and may depend on at most $O(p^{\delta_1})$ Brownian components, allowing leverage.
nodes.section: LSD of non-overlapping averaged TVA (ATVA) matrix

nodes.name: Assumption (A.iv)
nodes.statement: there exists $C_2<\infty$ such that for all $p$ and all $l$, the individual volatilities $\sigma_t^{(l)} = \sqrt{(\gamma_t)^2\sum_{k=1}^p(\Lambda_{lk})^2}\in (1/C_2, C_2)$ for all $t\in [0,1]$ almost surely; in addition, $(\gamma_t)$ converges uniformly to a nonzero process $(\gamma_t^*)$ that is piecewise continuous with finitely many jumps almost surely;
nodes.statement_short: Individual volatilities are bounded and $(\gamma_t)$ converges uniformly to a piecewise-continuous limit $(\gamma_t^*)$.
nodes.section: LSD of non-overlapping averaged TVA (ATVA) matrix

nodes.name: Assumption (A.v)
nodes.statement: there exists $C_3<\infty$ and $0\leq \delta_2 <1/2$ such that for all $p$, $||\text{ICV}|| \leq C_3p^{\delta_2}$ almost surely;
nodes.statement_short: The spectral norm of the ICV grows at most like $p^{\delta_2}$ with $\delta_2<1/2$.
nodes.section: LSD of non-overlapping averaged TVA (ATVA) matrix

nodes.name: Assumption (A.vi)
nodes.statement: the $\delta_1$ in \eqref{asm:bdd_gamma} and $\delta_2$ in \eqref{asm:bdd_ICV} satisfy that $\delta_1 + \delta_2 <1/2$;
nodes.statement_short: The two growth exponents jointly satisfy $\delta_1+\delta_2<1/2$.
nodes.section: LSD of non-overlapping averaged TVA (ATVA) matrix

nodes.name: Assumption (A.vii)
nodes.statement: almost surely, as $p\to\infty$, the ESD of $\bbSigma = \bLambda\bLambda^{\mathrm{T}}$ converges in distribution to a probability distribution $\breve{H}$;
nodes.statement_short: The ESD of $\bLambda\bLambda^{\mathrm{T}}$ has a limit $\breve{H}$.
nodes.section: LSD of non-overlapping averaged TVA (ATVA) matrix

nodes.name: Assumption (A.viii)
nodes.statement: $N = \lfloor n/2 \rfloor$ with $\lim_{p\to \infty} p/N \to \rho \in (0, \infty)$;
nodes.statement_short: High-dimensional regime: $p/N\to\rho\in(0,\infty)$.
nodes.section: LSD of non-overlapping averaged TVA (ATVA) matrix

nodes.name: Assumption (A.ix)
nodes.statement: the transaction durations are equally spaced in each time interval $(t_{i-1}, t_i]$, that is, $\Delta s_{i,j}: = s_{T_{i-1}+j} - s_{T_{i-1}+j-1} = 1/(nL_i)$ for $j = 1,\cdots, L_i$ and $i = 1,\cdots, n$;
nodes.statement_short: Transaction times are equally spaced inside each recording interval.
nodes.section: LSD of non-overlapping averaged TVA (ATVA) matrix

nodes.name: Assumption (A.x)
nodes.statement: $\{L_{1},\cdots, L_n\}$ is a sequence of independent positive integers independent of $(\bX_t)$ with $E(\frac{1}{L_i}) = f_{1, t_i}$ and $E(\frac{1}{L_i^2}) = f_{2, t_i}$ for $i = 1, \cdots, n$, where $f_{1, t}$ and $f_{2, t}$ are c\`{a}dl\`{a}g functions satisfying $\lim\limits_{n\to\infty} f_{1, t} = f_{1, t}^*$, $\lim\limits_{n\to\infty} f_{2, t} = f_{2, t}^*$ for $t\in [0,1]$.
nodes.statement_short: The transaction counts $L_i$ are independent of the price with càdlàg moment functions $f_{1,t},f_{2,t}$ converging to limits.
nodes.section: LSD of non-overlapping averaged TVA (ATVA) matrix

nodes.name: Theorem 2.1 (LSD of the non-overlapping ATVA matrix)
nodes.statement: Suppose that Assumptions \eqref{asm:class_c}--\eqref{asm:moment_L} hold. Then, almost surely, the ESDs of ICV and $\cA_N$ converge to probability distributions $H$ and $F^{\cA}$, respectively, where \begin{equation} H(x)=\breve{H}(x/\theta), ~~~ \textrm{for all } x\geq 0 ~ \textrm{with} ~ \theta=\int_0^1 (\gamma_t^*)^2 dt, \end{equation} and $F^{\cA}$ and $H$ are related as follows: \[ m_{\cA}(z) = \int_{\tau\in \mathbb{R}} \frac{1}{\tilde{\theta}_f/\theta\cdot\tau(1 - \rho(1 + zm_{\cA}(z))) - z}dH(\tau), ~~~~ \textrm{for} ~ z\in \mathbb{C}^+, \] where $\tilde{\theta}_f = \int_0^1 (\dfrac 13 + \dfrac 16 f_{2,s}^*)(\gamma_s^*)^2ds$ and $m_{\cA}(z)$ denotes the Stieltjes transform of $F^{\cA}$.
nodes.statement_short: The LSD of the ATVA matrix is tied to that of the ICV by a Marčenko–Pastur-type equation whose scale $\tilde\theta_f/\theta$ still involves the transaction counts.
nodes.section: LSD of non-overlapping averaged TVA (ATVA) matrix
conclusions: almost surely, the ESDs of ICV and $\cA_N$ converge to probability distributions $H$ and $F^{\cA}$, respectively

$F^{\cA}$ and $H$ are related as follows: \[ m_{\cA}(z) = \int_{\tau\in \mathbb{R}} \frac{1}{\tilde{\theta}_f/\theta\cdot\tau(1 - \rho(1 + zm_{\cA}(z))) - z}dH(\tau), ~~~~ \textrm{for} ~ z\in \mathbb{C}^+, \] where $\tilde{\theta}_f = \int_0^1 (\dfrac 13 + \dfrac 16 f_{2,s}^*)(\gamma_s^*)^2ds$ and $m_{\cA}(z)$ denotes the Stieltjes transform of $F^{\cA}$.

nodes.name: Remark 2.1 (inconsistency of the scaling factor under multiple transactions)
nodes.statement: Note that if $(\bX_t)$ belongs to class $\mathcal{C}$ then the ICV matrix can be written as $\ICV = \int_0^1 \gamma_t^2 dt\cdot \bbSigma$, where $\bbSigma = \bLambda\bLambda^{\mathrm{T}}$. When $L_i \equiv 1$, Theorem 2 of \cite{ZhengandLi2011} shows that the LSDs of $\wt{\bSigma}$ and $\bbSigma$ are related through the Mar\v{c}enko--Pastur equation (see \eqref{eq: converfence of proposition A1}), and $2\sum_{i=1}^N|\Delta \bX_{2i}|^2/p $ is a consistent estimator of $\theta=\int_0^1 (\gamma_t^*)^2 dt$. Throughout the proof of Theorem \ref{thm:LSD_TVA} in this paper, the LSDs of $\wt{\bSigma}$ and $\bbSigma$ are related through the Mar\v{c}enko--Pastur equation (see Proposition \ref{prop: convergence of tilde sigma} in the appendix); however, $2\sum_{i=1}^N|\Delta \bX_{2i}|^2/p $ is no longer consistent with $\theta$ in a general setting when $L_i \equiv 1$ is not satisfied. Hence, a non-overlapping A-ATVA matrix, $\wt{\cA}_N$, is proposed in Corollary \ref{cor:LSD_ATVA}, the LSD of which depends solely on that of the ICV matrix.
nodes.statement_short: When $L_i\not\equiv 1$ the usual estimator of $\theta$ is no longer consistent, motivating the adjusted A-ATVA matrix.
nodes.section: LSD of non-overlapping averaged TVA (ATVA) matrix

nodes.name: Remark 2.2 (U-shaped intraday transaction intensity)
nodes.statement: Moreover, observe that the stock intraday volatility tends to be U-shaped, which implies that the numbers of transactions at opening and closing of the market tend to be much larger than the numbers in the middle of the day. Thus, if Assumption \eqref{asm:moment_L} is further taken to be piecewise constant, Corollary \ref{cor:LSD_ATVA} (see below) holds.
nodes.statement_short: Intraday trading intensity is U-shaped, which makes the piecewise-constant form of Assumption (A.x) realistic.
nodes.section: LSD of non-overlapping averaged TVA (ATVA) matrix

nodes.name: Adjusted ATVA (A-ATVA) matrix $\wt{\cA}_N$
nodes.statement: If we further suppose that $(f_{2, s}^*)$ is piecewise constant, that is, there exist constant numbers $\eta_1,\cdots,\eta_K$ for $K<\infty$ such that \[ f_{2, s}^* = \sum_{i=1}^K \eta_i \mathrm{I}\{s\in(a_{i-1}, a_i]\}, \] where $(0, 1] = \sum_{i =1}^K (a_{i-1}, a_i]$ and $0 = a_{0} <a_1<\cdots<a_K = 1$, then we define the adjusted ATVA (A-ATVA) matrix as \[ \wt{\cA}_N := \frac{1}{p}\sum_{i = 1}^K \left( \dfrac13 + \frac{1}{6(\ell_i - \ell_{i-1})}\sum_{j = \ell_{i-1}+1}^{\ell_i}\frac{1}{L_j^2}\right)^{-1} \sum_{m = \lfloor (\ell_{i-1} + 1)/2\rfloor + 1}^{\lfloor\ell_i/2\rfloor}|\Delta\wbX_{2m}|^2 \cdot \wt{\bSigma}, \] where $\ell_i = \max\limits_{0\leq j\leq n}j/n\leq a_i$, provided that $\min\limits_{1\leq i \leq K}n(a_i - a_{i-1})\geq 3$.
nodes.statement_short: Rescales the ATVA matrix piecewise by $(1/3+\frac{1}{6}\overline{L^{-2}})^{-1}$ so that the transaction-count effect cancels.

nodes.name: Corollary 2.1 (LSD of the A-ATVA matrix)
nodes.statement: Under the assumptions of Theorem \ref{thm:LSD_TVA}, if we further suppose that $(f_{2, s}^*)$ is piecewise constant, then, almost surely, the ESD of $\wt{\cA}_N $ converges to a probability distribution $F^{\wt{\cA}}$, which is determined by $H$ through the Stieltjes transform via the Mar\v{c}enko--Pastur equation \[ m_{\wt{\cA}}(z) = \int \frac{1}{\tau(1 - \rho(1 + zm_{\wt{\cA}}(z))) - z}dH(\tau), ~~~~ \textrm{for} ~ z\in \mathbb{C}^+, \] where $m_{\wt{\cA}}(z)$ is the Stieltjes transform of $F^{\wt{\cA}}$.
nodes.statement_short: For piecewise-constant $(f_{2,s}^*)$ the A-ATVA matrix satisfies the plain Marčenko–Pastur equation, so its LSD depends only on that of the ICV.

nodes.name: Additive microstructure noise model
nodes.statement: Instead of the latent process $(\bX_t)$, the observed contaminated process $(\bY_t)$ is usually assumed to follow the additive model \begin{equation} \bY_{t} = \bX_{t} + \bm\varepsilon_{t}, \hspace{1cm} \text{for~} t\in [0,1], \end{equation} where $\bm\varepsilon_{t} = (\varepsilon_{t}^{(1)}, \cdots,\varepsilon_{t}^{(p)})^\mathrm{T}$ denotes the noise process.
nodes.statement_short: Observed prices equal latent log prices plus an additive noise process, $\bY_t=\bX_t+\bm\varepsilon_t$.

nodes.name: Pre-averaged observation $\twbV_i$
nodes.statement: We further introduce the following notation: \[ \hspace{1cm}\twbV_i:= \frac{1}{h}\sum_{j = 1}^{h}\widebar{\bV}_{(i-1)h+j} ~~~\text{and}~~~\Delta\twbV_{2i} = \twbV_{2i} - \twbV_{2i - 1}.\]
nodes.statement_short: Averages $h$ consecutive averaged observations into one pre-averaged block, with block return $\Delta\twbV_{2i}$.

nodes.name: Pre-averaging averaged TVA (PA-ATVA) matrix $\mbB_M$
nodes.statement: Next, we define an averaged version of the TVA matrix as follows. Let $h = \lfloor\xi n^{\beta}\rfloor$ with $\xi \in (0,\infty)$ and $\beta \in (1/2,1)$. Take $\hv = \lfloor n/(2h)\rfloor $. The PA-ATVA matrix is then defined as \begin{equation*} \mbB_{\hv}:= 3\frac{\sum_{i=1}^\hv|\Delta\twbY_{2i}|^2}{\hv}\cdot \sum_{i=1}^\hv\frac{\Delta\twbY_{2i}(\Delta\twbY_{2i})^{\mathrm{T}}}{|\Delta\twbY_{2i}|^2} = 3\frac{\sum_{i=1}^\hv|\Delta\twbY_{2i}|^2}{p}\cdot\hbSigma, \end{equation*}
nodes.statement_short: The PA-ATVA matrix applies the TVA construction to pre-averaged block returns with window $h=\lfloor\xi n^\beta\rfloor$, $\beta\in(1/2,1)$.

nodes.name: Self-normalized pre-averaged matrix $\hbSigma$
nodes.statement: where \begin{equation} \hbSigma := \frac{p}{\hv} \sum_{i=1}^\hv\frac{\Delta\twbY_{2i}(\Delta\twbY_{2i})^{\mathrm{T}}}{|\Delta\twbY_{2i}|^2}. \end{equation}

nodes.name: $\rho$-mixing coefficients
nodes.statement: For a stationary time series $(U_k),k\in \mathbb{Z}$, let $\mathcal{F}_j^\ell$ be the $\sigma$-field generated by the random variables $(U_k: -\infty\leq j\leq k \leq \ell\leq\infty)$. The $\rho$-mixing coefficients are defined as \[\rho(r) = \sup\limits_{f\in\mathcal{L}^2(\mathcal{F}_{-\infty}^0) ,~~ g\in \mathcal{L}^2(\mathcal{F}_{r}^\infty)} |\begin{rm}Corr\end{rm}(f,g)|, \hspace{0.5cm} \text{for} \hspace{0.5cm} r\in\mathbb{N},\] where, for any probability space $\Omega$, $\mathcal{L}^2(\Omega)$ refers to the space of square-integrable, $\Omega$-measurable random variables.
nodes.statement_short: $\rho(r)$ is the maximal correlation between square-integrable functionals of the past and of the $r$-shifted future.

nodes.name: Assumption (B.i)
nodes.statement: For all $j= 1,\cdots,p$, the noise $(\varepsilon_t^{(j)})$ is a stationary time series with mean 0 and has bounded $4\ell$th moments and $\rho$-mixing coefficients $\rho^{(j)}(r)$ satisfying $\max_{j=1,\cdots,p} \rho^{(j)}(r) = O(r^{-\ell})$ for some integer $\ell>2$;
nodes.statement_short: The noise is stationary, centred, has bounded $4\ell$th moments and polynomially decaying $\rho$-mixing coefficients.

nodes.name: Assumption (B.ii)
nodes.statement: $h =\lfloor \xi n^{\beta} \rfloor$ for some $\xi\in(0,\infty)$ and $\beta \in ((3+\ell)/(2\ell +2), 1)$, and $\hv = \lfloor n/(2h)\rfloor$ satisfy that $\lim_{p\to\infty} p/\hv = c >0$, where $\ell$ is the integer in Assumption \eqref{asm:error};

nodes.name: Assumption (B.iii)
nodes.statement: there exists a constant $L^*<\infty$ such that $\sup\limits_{1\leq i \leq n} L_i\leq L^*$, almost surely;

nodes.name: Assumption (B.iv)
nodes.statement: $\max\limits_{1\leq i \leq n} n(s_{T_i} - s_{T_{i-1}}) \to 1$, almost surely, as $n\to \infty$.

nodes.name: Theorem 2.2 (LSD of the PA-ATVA matrix under microstructure noise)
nodes.statement: Suppose that Assumptions \eqref{asm:class_c}-\eqref{asm:LSD_bH} and \eqref{asm:error}-\eqref{asm:interval} hold. Then, as $p\to\infty$, the ESDs of ICV and $\mbB_M$ converge almost surely to probability distributions $H$ and $F^{\mbB}$, respectively, where $H$ satisfies \eqref{eq: determine of H} and $F^{\mbB}$ is determined by $H$ in that its Stieltjes transform, $m_{\mbB}(z)$, satisfies the Mar\v{c}enko--Pastur equation, \begin{equation} m_{\mbB}(z) = \int_{\tau\in \mathbb{R}} \frac{1}{\tau(1 - c(1 + zm_{\mbB}(z))) - z}dH(\tau),\hspace{0.2cm}\text{for}~z\in \mathbb{C^{+}}. \end{equation}
nodes.statement_short: Pre-averaging removes both the noise and the multiple-transaction effect: the LSD of $\mbB_M$ depends on the ICV alone through the Marčenko–Pastur equation.

nodes.name: PA-ATVA matrix under asynchronous trading $\mbB_M^*$
nodes.statement: With asynchronous trading, the average of multiple observations at each recording time $t_i$ is denoted as \[ \ol{\bV}_i^* = \left(\sum_{j=1}^{L_i^{(1)}}\frac{1}{L_i^{(1)}}V_{i,j}^{(1)}, \cdots, \sum_{j=1}^{L_i^{(p)}}\frac{1}{L_i^{(p)}}V_{i,j}^{(p)} \right)^{\mT}, \] and the pre-averaging averaged observation becomes \[ \twbV_i^* = \frac{1}{h}\sum_{j = 1}^{h}\widebar{\bV}_{(i-1)h+j}^*, \] for $i = 1,\cdots, n$. Using the above notation, the PA-ATVA matrix is then rewritten as \[ \mbB_M^* = 3\frac{\sum_{i=1}^\hv|\Delta\twbY_{2i}^*|^2}{\hv}\cdot \sum_{i=1}^\hv\frac{\Delta\twbY_{2i}^*(\Delta\twbY_{2i}^*)^{\mathrm{T}}}{|\Delta\twbY_{2i}^*|^2}. \]
nodes.statement_short: Stock-by-stock averaging when each stock $q$ has its own transaction count $L_i^{(q)}$, giving the asynchronous PA-ATVA matrix $\mbB_M^*$.

Further, assume that $\max\limits_{1\leq i \leq n, 1\leq q\leq p} nh(s_{T_i}^{(q)} - t_i) \to 0 $, almost surely. Then, as $p\to\infty$, the ESDs of ICV and $\mbB_M^*$ converge almost surely to probability distributions $H$ and $F^{\mbB^*}$, respectively, where $H$ satisfies \eqref{eq: determine of H} and $F^{\mbB^*}$ is determined by $H$ in that its Stieltjes transform $m_{\mbB^*}(z)$ satisfies the Mar\v{c}enko--Pastur equation, \begin{equation} m_{\mbB^*}(z) = \int_{\tau\in \mathbb{R}} \frac{1}{\tau(1 - c(1 + zm_{\mbB^*}(z))) - z}dH(\tau),\hspace{0.2cm}\text{for}~z\in \mathbb{C^{+}}. \end{equation}
nodes.statement_short: The same Marčenko–Pastur relation survives when the transaction counts differ across stocks, provided $nh(s_{T_i}^{(q)}-t_i)\to0$.

nodes.name: Nonlinear shrinkage (NS) estimator of the ICV matrix
nodes.statement: Suppose that we observe high-frequency multiple noisy observations $\{\bY_{t_i}\}$ during time period $[T - \tau, T]$ at current time $T$, for $\tau\geq 1$. We construct matrix $\hbSigma$ based on observations $\{\bY_{t_i}\}$ over time period $[T - \tau ,T]$ and estimator $\hat\theta_p$ based on observations $\{\bY_{t_i}\}$ during time interval $[T - 1, T]$. We denote the spectral decomposition of matrix $\hbSigma$ by \[ \hbSigma = \bP_{T - \tau, T}\wt{\bLambda}_{T - \tau, T} \bP_{T - \tau, T}^{\mT}, \] where the eigenmatrix $\bP_{T - \tau, T} = (\bp_{T - \tau, T}[1], \cdots, \bp_{T - \tau, T}[p])$, whose $i$th column is the eigenvector of $\hbSigma $, and $\wt{\bLambda}_{T - \tau, T} = \diag \{ \wt{\lambda}_1 ,\cdots, \wt{\lambda}_p\}$ is a diagonal matrix with non-increasing eigenvalues $\wt{\lambda}_1\geq \cdots \geq \wt{\lambda}_p$. To construct an NS estimator of $\bbSigma$, we retain the eigenmatrix $\bP_{T-\tau, T}$ and consider a class of estimators of the form: \[ \bP_{T-\tau, T} {\bf D} \bP_{T-\tau, T}^{\mT}, \] where $D = \diag( d_1, \cdots, d_p)$ is diagonal. In order to measure the distance between two matrices, we adopt the Frobenius norm. The objective is to find the diagonal matrix ${\bf D}$ that solves the optimization problem \[ \min\limits_{{\bf D} ~~\text{diag}}\| \bP_{T - \tau, T} {\bf D} \bP_{T - \tau, T}^{\mT} - \bbSigma\|_F. \] By elementary calculation, the solution is \[D^{or} = \diag(d_1^{or},\cdots, d_p^{or}), \] where \begin{equation} d_i^{or} = (\bp_{T - \tau, T}[i])^{\mT} \bbSigma \bp_{T - \tau, T}[i]. \end{equation} Therefore, we propose the following nonlinear shrinkage (NS) estimator for ICV: \[ \wh{\bSigma}_{NS}: = \hat{\theta}_p \cdot \wh{\bXi}_{NS}, \] where $\wh\bXi_{NS} = \bP_{T - \tau, T} \diag(\wh{d_1^{or}},\cdots, \wh{d_p^{or}}) \bP_{T-\tau ,T}^{\mT}$, and $\wh{d_i^{or}}$ is an estimator of $d_i^{or}$, solved by the algorithm proposed by \cite{LedoitandWolf2017}.
nodes.statement_short: Keep the eigenvectors of $\hbSigma$, replace its eigenvalues by the Frobenius-optimal oracle values $d_i^{or}$, and rescale by $\hat\theta_p$.
input: high-frequency multiple noisy observations $\{\bY_{t_i}\}$ during time period $[T - \tau, T]$
estimator $\hat\theta_p$ based on observations $\{\bY_{t_i}\}$ during time interval $[T - 1, T]$

nodes.name: Construct $\hbSigma$ and $\hat\theta_p$
nodes.statement: We construct matrix $\hbSigma$ based on observations $\{\bY_{t_i}\}$ over time period $[T - \tau ,T]$ and estimator $\hat\theta_p$ based on observations $\{\bY_{t_i}\}$ during time interval $[T - 1, T]$.
nodes.statement_short: Build the self-normalized matrix on $[T-\tau,T]$ and the scale estimator on the last day.

nodes.name: Spectral decomposition of $\hbSigma$
nodes.statement: We denote the spectral decomposition of matrix $\hbSigma$ by \[ \hbSigma = \bP_{T - \tau, T}\wt{\bLambda}_{T - \tau, T} \bP_{T - \tau, T}^{\mT}, \] where the eigenmatrix $\bP_{T - \tau, T} = (\bp_{T - \tau, T}[1], \cdots, \bp_{T - \tau, T}[p])$, whose $i$th column is the eigenvector of $\hbSigma $, and $\wt{\bLambda}_{T - \tau, T} = \diag \{ \wt{\lambda}_1 ,\cdots, \wt{\lambda}_p\}$ is a diagonal matrix with non-increasing eigenvalues $\wt{\lambda}_1\geq \cdots \geq \wt{\lambda}_p$.
nodes.statement_short: Diagonalize $\hbSigma$ into eigenmatrix $\bP_{T-\tau,T}$ and eigenvalues $\wt\lambda_i$.

nodes.name: Restrict to rotation-equivariant candidates
nodes.statement: To construct an NS estimator of $\bbSigma$, we retain the eigenmatrix $\bP_{T-\tau, T}$ and consider a class of estimators of the form: \[ \bP_{T-\tau, T} {\bf D} \bP_{T-\tau, T}^{\mT}, \] where $D = \diag( d_1, \cdots, d_p)$ is diagonal.
nodes.statement_short: Search only over estimators that keep the eigenvectors and change the diagonal $\bf D$.

nodes.name: Minimize the Frobenius distance
nodes.statement: In order to measure the distance between two matrices, we adopt the Frobenius norm. The objective is to find the diagonal matrix ${\bf D}$ that solves the optimization problem \[ \min\limits_{{\bf D} ~~\text{diag}}\| \bP_{T - \tau, T} {\bf D} \bP_{T - \tau, T}^{\mT} - \bbSigma\|_F. \]
nodes.statement_short: Choose $\bf D$ minimizing the Frobenius distance to $\bbSigma$.

nodes.name: Oracle eigenvalues $d_i^{or}$
nodes.statement: By elementary calculation, the solution is \[D^{or} = \diag(d_1^{or},\cdots, d_p^{or}), \] where \begin{equation} d_i^{or} = (\bp_{T - \tau, T}[i])^{\mT} \bbSigma \bp_{T - \tau, T}[i]. \end{equation}
nodes.statement_short: The minimizer is the quadratic form of $\bbSigma$ in each eigenvector.

nodes.name: Return the NS estimator
nodes.statement: Therefore, we propose the following nonlinear shrinkage (NS) estimator for ICV: \[ \wh{\bSigma}_{NS}: = \hat{\theta}_p \cdot \wh{\bXi}_{NS}, \] where $\wh\bXi_{NS} = \bP_{T - \tau, T} \diag(\wh{d_1^{or}},\cdots, \wh{d_p^{or}}) \bP_{T-\tau ,T}^{\mT}$, and $\wh{d_i^{or}}$ is an estimator of $d_i^{or}$, solved by the algorithm proposed by \cite{LedoitandWolf2017}.
nodes.statement_short: Return $\hat\theta_p\cdot\bP\diag(\wh{d_i^{or}})\bP^{\mT}$, with $\wh{d_i^{or}}$ from Ledoit and Wolf's QuEST routine.

nodes.name: Frobenius-optimal diagonal shrinkage problem
nodes.statement: The objective is to find the diagonal matrix ${\bf D}$ that solves the optimization problem \[ \min\limits_{{\bf D} ~~\text{diag}}\| \bP_{T - \tau, T} {\bf D} \bP_{T - \tau, T}^{\mT} - \bbSigma\|_F. \]
nodes.statement_short: Minimize $\|\bP\,{\bf D}\,\bP^{\mT}-\bbSigma\|_F$ over diagonal $\bf D$.

nodes.name: Averaged nonlinear shrinkage (ANS) estimator
nodes.statement: Suppose that we have tick-by-tick high-frequency observations $\{\bY_{l_i}\}$ over time period $[T - \tau, T]$ at current time $T$. First, the estimator $\hat{\theta}_p = 3\sum_{i=1}^M |\Delta \twbY_{2i}|^2/p$ can be established based on high-frequency data during time interval $[T - 1, T]$. Suppose that there are in total $M_{\tau} = \tau \cdot M$ averaged noisy increments $\Delta \twbY_{2j}, j = 1, \cdots, M_{\tau}$, over time period $[T - \tau, T]$, in which the overnight increments are excluded and there are $M$ increments each day. Next, we permute the increments $B$ times. At the $k$th permutation, we split the increments $\Delta \twbY^{(k)}$ into two parts, say $\Delta \twbY^{(k)} = (\Delta \twbY^{(k)}_1, \Delta \twbY^{(k)}_2)$, for $k = 1,\cdots, B$, with $\Delta \twbY^{(k)}_\ell$ having size $p\times M_{\tau_{\ell}}$ $(\ell = 1, 2)$ and $M_{\tau_1} + M_{\tau_2} = M_{\tau}$. We define \[ \hbSigma_{\ell}^{(k)} := \frac{p}{\hv_{\tau_{\ell}}}\sum_{i \in J_{\ell, k}}\frac{\Delta\twbY_{2i} (\Delta\twbY_{2i})^{\mathrm{T}}}{|\Delta\twbY_{2i}|^2}, \] where $J_{\ell, k} = \{i: \Delta \twbY_{2i} \in \Delta\twbY_{\ell}^{(k)}\}$ for $\ell = 1, 2$ and $k = 1, \cdots, B$. We denote the spectral decomposition of $\wt{\bXi}_1^{(k)}$ as \[ \wt{\bXi}_1^{(k)} = \bP_1^{(k)}\wt{\bLambda}_1^{(k)}(\bP_1^{(k)})^{\mT}, \] for $k = 1,\cdots, B$. Then the averaged nonlinear shrinkage (ANS) estimator of ICV is defined as \begin{equation*} \wh{\bSigma}_{\ANS}:= \hat{\theta}_p\cdot\frac{1}{B} \sum_{k=1}^B \hbSigma^{(k)}_{\ANS}, ~~\hbSigma^{(k)}_{\ANS} = \bP_1^{(k)} \diag((\bP_1^{(k)})^{\mT} \wt{\bXi}_2^{(k)}\bP_1^{(k)}) (\bP_1^{(k)})^{\mT}, \end{equation*} where $\diag(\bA)$ sets all non-diagonal elements of matrix $\bA$ to zero.
nodes.statement_short: Split the pre-averaged returns into two parts $B$ times, regularize the eigenvalues of one half with the other, and average over permutations.
input: tick-by-tick high-frequency observations $\{\bY_{l_i}\}$ over time period $[T - \tau, T]$
$M_{\tau} = \tau \cdot M$ averaged noisy increments $\Delta \twbY_{2j}, j = 1, \cdots, M_{\tau}$

nodes.name: Estimate the scale $\hat\theta_p$
nodes.statement: First, the estimator $\hat{\theta}_p = 3\sum_{i=1}^M |\Delta \twbY_{2i}|^2/p$ can be established based on high-frequency data during time interval $[T - 1, T]$.
nodes.statement_short: Compute $\hat\theta_p$ from the last day of data.

nodes.name: Collect the averaged increments
nodes.statement: Suppose that there are in total $M_{\tau} = \tau \cdot M$ averaged noisy increments $\Delta \twbY_{2j}, j = 1, \cdots, M_{\tau}$, over time period $[T - \tau, T]$, in which the overnight increments are excluded and there are $M$ increments each day.
nodes.statement_short: Gather the $M_\tau$ overnight-free pre-averaged increments over the training window.

nodes.name: Permute the increments $B$ times
nodes.statement: Next, we permute the increments $B$ times.
nodes.statement_short: Repeat the splitting $B$ times over random permutations.

nodes.name: Split each permutation into two parts
nodes.statement: At the $k$th permutation, we split the increments $\Delta \twbY^{(k)}$ into two parts, say $\Delta \twbY^{(k)} = (\Delta \twbY^{(k)}_1, \Delta \twbY^{(k)}_2)$, for $k = 1,\cdots, B$, with $\Delta \twbY^{(k)}_\ell$ having size $p\times M_{\tau_{\ell}}$ $(\ell = 1, 2)$ and $M_{\tau_1} + M_{\tau_2} = M_{\tau}$.
nodes.statement_short: Divide the increments into two blocks of sizes $M_{\tau_1},M_{\tau_2}$.

nodes.name: Form the two self-normalized matrices
nodes.statement: We define \[ \hbSigma_{\ell}^{(k)} := \frac{p}{\hv_{\tau_{\ell}}}\sum_{i \in J_{\ell, k}}\frac{\Delta\twbY_{2i} (\Delta\twbY_{2i})^{\mathrm{T}}}{|\Delta\twbY_{2i}|^2}, \] where $J_{\ell, k} = \{i: \Delta \twbY_{2i} \in \Delta\twbY_{\ell}^{(k)}\}$ for $\ell = 1, 2$ and $k = 1, \cdots, B$.
nodes.statement_short: Build $\hbSigma_1^{(k)},\hbSigma_2^{(k)}$ from the two halves.

nodes.name: Diagonalize the first half
nodes.statement: We denote the spectral decomposition of $\wt{\bXi}_1^{(k)}$ as \[ \wt{\bXi}_1^{(k)} = \bP_1^{(k)}\wt{\bLambda}_1^{(k)}(\bP_1^{(k)})^{\mT}, \] for $k = 1,\cdots, B$.
nodes.statement_short: Take the eigenvectors $\bP_1^{(k)}$ of the first half.

nodes.name: Average the regularized estimators
nodes.statement: Then the averaged nonlinear shrinkage (ANS) estimator of ICV is defined as \begin{equation*} \wh{\bSigma}_{\ANS}:= \hat{\theta}_p\cdot\frac{1}{B} \sum_{k=1}^B \hbSigma^{(k)}_{\ANS}, ~~\hbSigma^{(k)}_{\ANS} = \bP_1^{(k)} \diag((\bP_1^{(k)})^{\mT} \wt{\bXi}_2^{(k)}\bP_1^{(k)}) (\bP_1^{(k)})^{\mT}, \end{equation*} where $\diag(\bA)$ sets all non-diagonal elements of matrix $\bA$ to zero.
nodes.statement_short: Regularize the eigenvalues of half 1 by the diagonal of half 2 in that basis, then average over the $B$ permutations.

nodes.name: Choice of the data-splitting location $M_{\tau_1}$
nodes.statement: To this end, $M_{\tau_1}$ is chosen using the following criterion, \begin{equation}\arg\min\limits_{\hv_{\tau_1}\in \mathcal{G}} \bigg| \bigg| \frac{1}{B} \sum_{k = 1}^B (\hbSigma^{(k)}_{\ANS} - \hbSigma_2^{(k)}) \bigg| \bigg|_F^2, \end{equation}
nodes.statement_short: Pick the split size minimizing the averaged Frobenius discrepancy between the regularized estimator and the second-half matrix.

nodes.name: Candidate set $\mathcal{G}$ for the split size
nodes.statement: where \begin{equation} \begin{split} \mathcal{G} = \bigg[2\hv_{\tau}^{1/2}, 0.2\hv_{\tau}, 0.4\hv_{\tau}, 0.6\hv_{\tau}, 0.8\hv_{\tau}, \hv_{\tau} - 2.5\hv_{\tau}^{1/2}, \hv_{\tau} - 1.5\hv_{\tau}^{1/2}\bigg] \end{split} \end{equation} is the candidate set for $\hv_{\tau_1}$, recommended by \cite{Lam2016} and \cite{Lametal2017}.
nodes.statement_short: Seven candidate split sizes recommended in the data-splitting shrinkage literature.

nodes.name: Mixed nonlinear shrinkage (MNS) estimator
nodes.statement: Suppose that we observe high-frequency data $\{\bY_t\}$ with multiple transactions during time period $[T - \tau, T]$. First, the matrix $\wt{\bXi}_{T-\tau, T-1}$ in \eqref{eq: definition of hbSigma} is constructed based on high-frequency data during time period $[T - \tau, T - 1]$, and its spectral decomposition is denoted as \[ \wt{\bXi}_{T-\tau, T - 1} = \bP_{T-\tau, T - 1}\wt{\bLambda}_{T-\tau, T - 1}(\bP_{T-\tau, T - 1})^{\mT}, \] where \[ \bP_{T-\tau, T - 1} = (\bp_{T-\tau, T - 1}[1], \cdots, \bp_{T-\tau, T - 1}[p]). \] Second, we set the eigenvectors $\bp_{T-\tau, T - 1}[k]$, $k = 1,\cdots, p$, to be given beforehand, and transform the averaged high-frequency data $\{\ol{\bY}_i\}$ during time period $[T - 1, T]$. That is, consider $\ol{\bY}_{k, i}^{**} = (\bp_{T-\tau, T - 1}[k])^{\mT}\ol{\bY}_i$ as the transformed averaged observations at recording time $t_i \in [T - 1,T]$, for $k = 1,\cdots, p, i = 0,\cdots, n$. Third, for each $k = 1,\cdots, p$, compute the averaging-pre-averaging estimator \[ \wh{d_i^{\APA}} = \frac{12}{k_n }\sum_{i = 0}^{n - k_n + 1}(\Delta_{i,k_n}^k\ol{\bY}_{k, i}^{**} )^2 - \frac{6}{\vartheta^2 n} \sum_{i = 0}^{n-1} (\ol{\bY}_{k, i + 1}^{**} - \ol{\bY}_{k, i}^{**})^2, \] where $k_n = \lfloor \vartheta n^{1/2}\rfloor, \vartheta>0$ and $\Delta_{i,k_n}^k\ol{\bY}_{k, i}^{**} = \sum_{j = 1}^{k_n -1} g(j/k_n)( \ol{\bY}_{k, i + j + 1}^{**} - \ol{\bY}_{k, i + j}^{**})$ with $g(x) = x\wedge (1-x)$, which is a consistent estimator of the integrated volatility of $(\ol{\bY}_{k, i}^{**})$ over $[T - 1, T]$ by given $\bU_{T - \tau, T - 1}$, see \cite{Jacodetal2009} and \cite{Liuetal2018}. Finally, our mixed nonlinear shrinkage (MNS) estimator of ICV is defined as \[ \wh{\bSigma}_{\MNS} = \bP_{T -\tau, T -1} \diag (\wh{d_1^{\APA}}, \cdots, \wh{d_p^{\APA}})\bP_{T -\tau, T -1}^{\mT}. \]
nodes.statement_short: Take eigenvectors from $[T-\tau,T-1]$, project the last day's averaged prices on them, and estimate each eigenvalue by an averaging-pre-averaging integrated-volatility estimator.
input: high-frequency data $\{\bY_t\}$ with multiple transactions during time period $[T - \tau, T]$

nodes.name: Build and diagonalize $\wt{\bXi}_{T-\tau,T-1}$
nodes.statement: First, the matrix $\wt{\bXi}_{T-\tau, T-1}$ in \eqref{eq: definition of hbSigma} is constructed based on high-frequency data during time period $[T - \tau, T - 1]$, and its spectral decomposition is denoted as \[ \wt{\bXi}_{T-\tau, T - 1} = \bP_{T-\tau, T - 1}\wt{\bLambda}_{T-\tau, T - 1}(\bP_{T-\tau, T - 1})^{\mT}, \] where \[ \bP_{T-\tau, T - 1} = (\bp_{T-\tau, T - 1}[1], \cdots, \bp_{T-\tau, T - 1}[p]). \]
nodes.statement_short: Construct the self-normalized matrix on $[T-\tau,T-1]$ and take its eigenvectors.

nodes.name: Project the last day's averaged prices
nodes.statement: Second, we set the eigenvectors $\bp_{T-\tau, T - 1}[k]$, $k = 1,\cdots, p$, to be given beforehand, and transform the averaged high-frequency data $\{\ol{\bY}_i\}$ during time period $[T - 1, T]$. That is, consider $\ol{\bY}_{k, i}^{**} = (\bp_{T-\tau, T - 1}[k])^{\mT}\ol{\bY}_i$ as the transformed averaged observations at recording time $t_i \in [T - 1,T]$, for $k = 1,\cdots, p, i = 0,\cdots, n$.
nodes.statement_short: Transform the averaged prices of $[T-1,T]$ onto each fixed eigenvector.

nodes.name: Averaging-pre-averaging eigenvalue estimator
nodes.statement: Third, for each $k = 1,\cdots, p$, compute the averaging-pre-averaging estimator \[ \wh{d_i^{\APA}} = \frac{12}{k_n }\sum_{i = 0}^{n - k_n + 1}(\Delta_{i,k_n}^k\ol{\bY}_{k, i}^{**} )^2 - \frac{6}{\vartheta^2 n} \sum_{i = 0}^{n-1} (\ol{\bY}_{k, i + 1}^{**} - \ol{\bY}_{k, i}^{**})^2, \] where $k_n = \lfloor \vartheta n^{1/2}\rfloor, \vartheta>0$ and $\Delta_{i,k_n}^k\ol{\bY}_{k, i}^{**} = \sum_{j = 1}^{k_n -1} g(j/k_n)( \ol{\bY}_{k, i + j + 1}^{**} - \ol{\bY}_{k, i + j}^{**})$ with $g(x) = x\wedge (1-x)$, which is a consistent estimator of the integrated volatility of $(\ol{\bY}_{k, i}^{**})$ over $[T - 1, T]$ by given $\bU_{T - \tau, T - 1}$, see \cite{Jacodetal2009} and \cite{Liuetal2018}.
nodes.statement_short: Estimate each projected integrated volatility by a pre-averaging estimator with noise correction.

nodes.name: Return the MNS estimator
nodes.statement: Finally, our mixed nonlinear shrinkage (MNS) estimator of ICV is defined as \[ \wh{\bSigma}_{\MNS} = \bP_{T -\tau, T -1} \diag (\wh{d_1^{\APA}}, \cdots, \wh{d_p^{\APA}})\bP_{T -\tau, T -1}^{\mT}. \]
nodes.statement_short: Reassemble $\bP\diag(\wh{d_i^{\APA}})\bP^{\mT}$.

nodes.name: U-shaped stochastic covolatility process used in simulations
nodes.statement: We take the following U-shaped stochastic process $(\gamma_t)$ as \begin{equation} d\gamma_t = -\rho(\gamma_t - \mu_t)dt + \sigma d\widetilde{W}_t, \hspace{0.5cm}\text{for} \hspace{0.5cm} t\in[0,1], \end{equation} where $\rho = 10, \sigma = 0.05, \mu_t = 2\sqrt{0.0009 + 0.0008\cos(2\pi t)}$, and the process $\widetilde{W}_t = \sum_{i=1}^p W_t^{(i)}/\sqrt{p} $ with $W_t^{(i)}$ being the $i$th component of the Brownian motion $(\bW_t)$ that derives the price process.
nodes.statement_short: An Ornstein–Uhlenbeck-type $(\gamma_t)$ with U-shaped mean reversion, driven by the average of the Brownian components.

nodes.name: Simulation model for the latent log price
nodes.statement: The latent log price process $(\bX_t)$ follows \begin{equation} d\bX_t = \gamma_t\bLambda d\bW_t. \end{equation}
nodes.statement_short: Driftless class-$\mathcal{C}$ price process $d\bX_t=\gamma_t\bLambda d\bW_t$ used throughout the simulations.

nodes.name: A-ATVA versus sample covariance matrix under Poisson transaction counts
nodes.statement: In this subsection, we compare the ESD of the A-ATVA matrix $\mbA_N$ and that of the sample covariance matrix $\bS_N$ with i.i.d. samples drawn from the ICV matrix, that is, $\bS_{N} = 1/N \sum_{i=1}^N (\ICV)^{1/2} \bZ_i \bZ_i^{\mT} (\ICV)^{1/2}$, where $\bZ_i \overset{i.i.d.}{\sim} N(0, \bI)$ and $N = \lfloor n /2\rfloor$. It is well known that the LSDs of a sample covariance matrix $\bS_N$ and the underlying population covariance matrix ICV are related through the Mar\v{c}enko--Pastur equation from Theorem 1.1 of \cite{Silverstein1995}, which coincides with the result of Corollary \ref{cor:LSD_ATVA}. We set $p = 100$ and $n = 390$, which represents the case where 100 stocks are recorded per minute within one trading day. Figure \ref{fig: application of theorem 1} illustrates the simulation result when the number of multiple transactions $L_i - 1, i =1,\cdots, n$, are i.i.d. generated from a Poisson distribution with parameter 5, Poisson (5).
nodes.statement_short: With $p=100$, $n=390$ and $L_i-1\sim$ Poisson(5), the ESDs of $\mbA_N$ and of the i.i.d. sample covariance matrix agree.

nodes.name: A-ATVA under stock-specific transaction counts $L_i^{(q)}$
nodes.statement: The result of Corollary \ref{cor:LSD_ATVA} is further examined when $L_i^{(q)}$ (the number of transactions for stock $q$ during time interval $(t_{i-1}, t_i]$) varies for different $q = 1, \cdots, p$. For each $i = 1,\cdots, n$ and $q = 1,\cdots, p$, we generate $L_i^{(q)}$ independently from a discrete uniform distribution, $U[1,5]$, and set the underlying trading time to be equally spaced during each recording time. The resulting ESDs for the A-ATVA matrix $\mbA_N$ and sample covariance matrix $\bS_N$ are shown in Figure \ref{fig: application of theorem 1 ill}, and the maximum distances between two ESDs are reported in Table \ref{table: TVA fail discussion}, with $p/n = 10/39$ fixed but $n$ increasing.
nodes.statement_short: When each stock has its own $L_i^{(q)}\sim U[1,5]$, the two ESDs no longer match and the gap does not vanish as $n$ grows.

nodes.name: Empirical maximum distance between two ESDs
nodes.statement: The maximum distances between the two ESDs, $F^{\mbA_N}$ and $F^{\bS_N}$, can be estimated using the following formula \begin{equation} \max\limits_{x_1,\cdots,x_{2p}}|F^{\mbA_N}(x_i) -F^{\bS_N}(x_i) |, \end{equation} where $x_1,\cdots, x_{2p}$ are chosen to be equally spaced in the interval $[\min(\lambda(\mbA_N), \lambda(\bS_N) )$, $\max(\lambda(\mbA_N), \lambda(\bS_N) )]$, where $\lambda(\bA)$ denotes the spectral of any symmetric matrix $\bA$.
nodes.statement_short: Kolmogorov-type distance evaluated on $2p$ equally spaced points spanning the union of the two spectra.

nodes.name: LSD of the A-ATVA matrix under stock-specific transaction counts
nodes.statement: Thus, the limiting spectral of an A-ATVA matrix based on different values of $L_i^{(q)}$ remains an open problem.
nodes.statement_short: The limiting spectral distribution of the A-ATVA matrix when transaction counts vary across stocks is left unresolved.

nodes.name: Design I: common transaction counts across stocks
nodes.statement: Design \uppercase\expandafter{\romannumeral1}: For simplicity, $L_i^{(q)} = L_i$ for each stock $q$ within time interval $(t_{i-1}, t_i]$, where the $t_i$ values are arranged as an equally spaced grid in $[0,1]$. The $L_i$'s are generated independently from a Poisson distribution with parameter 20 for the first and the last hours within 6.5 hours of a trading day, and from a Poisson distribution with parameter 5 for the remaining trading hours. According to the simulation results, shown in Figure \ref{fig: application of theorem 2}, the two ESDs were very closely matched.
nodes.statement_short: Synchronous design with U-shaped Poisson transaction counts; the PA-ATVA and sample-covariance ESDs match.

nodes.name: Design II: highly asynchronous transaction counts
nodes.statement: Design \uppercase\expandafter{\romannumeral2}: In order to generate high-frequency data such as that commonly used in practice, we further simulated observations in a highly asynchronous setting. Based on Design \uppercase\expandafter{\romannumeral1}, we allowed variation of $L_i^{(q)}$, which is generated independently from a discrete uniform distribution within the interval $[1, L_i]$, for each $q = 1, \cdots, p$ and $i = 1, \cdots, n$. Figure \ref{fig: application of theorem 2b} displays the ESDs of matrices $\mbB_M$ and $\bS_M$ under Design \uppercase\expandafter{\romannumeral2}.
nodes.statement_short: Asynchronous design with $L_i^{(q)}\sim U[1,L_i]$; the PA-ATVA matrix still matches the sample covariance ESD.

nodes.name: Four covolatility settings for comparing the NS, ANS and MNS estimators
nodes.statement: We generated a two-day log price process $(\bX_t)$ using model \eqref{eq: simulation model}, except that matrix $\bLambda$ had the following four settings: \begin{itemize} \item Setting \uppercase\expandafter{\romannumeral1}: set $\bLambda = (0.5^{|i - j|})_{i,j = 1,\cdots,p}$ for two days; \item Setting \uppercase\expandafter{\romannumeral2}: set $\bLambda = (0.5^{|i - j|})_{i,j = 1,\cdots,p}$ and change the first three eigenvalues of $\bLambda$ to be $15, 10, 5$, and further rescale the spectral of $\bLambda$ to satisfy $\tr(\bLambda\bLambda^{\mT}) = p$; \item Setting \uppercase\expandafter{\romannumeral3}: set $\bLambda$ as in Setting \uppercase\expandafter{\romannumeral2}, except that the first three eigenvalues of $\bLambda$ are set to be $15, 10, 5$ for day 1, and the first three eigenvalues of $\bLambda$ are $30, 10, 5$ for day 2. \item Setting \uppercase\expandafter{\romannumeral4}: set $\bLambda$ as in Setting \uppercase\expandafter{\romannumeral2}, except that the first three eigenvalues of $\bLambda$ are set to be $15, 10, 5$ for day 1, and the first eigenvalue of $\bLambda$ is $30$ for day 2. \end{itemize} We constructed high-frequency noisy data $(\bY_{t_i})$ using Design \uppercase\expandafter{\romannumeral2}, described in subsection \ref{subsec: PA-ATVA}, obtaining $23400\times 2$ observations for $p = 30$ or $100$ stocks, respectively. The pre-averaging window length $h$ in the PA-ATVA matrix $\mbB_M$ and window length $k_n$ in the MNS estimator $\wh{\bSigma}_{\MNS}$ were taken to be $\lfloor n^{0.55}\rfloor = 252$ and $\lfloor 0.75n^{1/2}\rfloor = 114$, respectively. For the ANS estimator $\wh{\bSigma}_{\ANS}$, we performed $B = 50$ permutations and compared all the simulation results under the seven data partition criteria given in \eqref{eq: nonlinear shrnkage criterion}. We denote ANS $i, i = 1,\cdots, 7$, when the data partition criterion $i$ is adopted as in \eqref{eq: critia for selection of n1}. For any matrix $\mathcal{\bm Q}$, we defined the relative Frobenius loss (RFL) as $||\mathcal{\bm Q}- \ICV||_F/||\ICV||_F$. For each setting, we repeated the simulations 1000 times. The means and standard deviations for the RFL of these estimators are presented in Table \ref{table: compare the nonlinear shrinkage}.
nodes.statement_short: Two-day simulations with flat, spiked, and day-changing spiked $\bLambda$, comparing relative Frobenius losses over 1000 replications.

nodes.name: Relative Frobenius loss (RFL)
nodes.statement: For any matrix $\mathcal{\bm Q}$, we defined the relative Frobenius loss (RFL) as $||\mathcal{\bm Q}- \ICV||_F/||\ICV||_F$.

nodes.name: Simulation findings for the three NS estimators
nodes.statement: As shown in Table \ref{table: compare the nonlinear shrinkage}, NS and ANS7 with small error mean performed better than the other estimators for Setting \uppercase\expandafter{\romannumeral1}, where the underlying covolatility structure was stable and no spikes were considered. However, when the spiked model of the ICV matrix or structure changes were considered, as in Setting \uppercase\expandafter{\romannumeral2}, \uppercase\expandafter{\romannumeral3}, and \uppercase\expandafter{\romannumeral4}, the MNS estimator outperformed the other estimators in terms of both mean and standard deviation. Comparing all the ANS estimators with different choices of data splitting criteria, the ANS estimator tended to have better performance when the first data set was larger. However, generally speaking, the MNS estimator was more efficient and robust when the structure changed or under factor models.
nodes.statement_short: NS/ANS7 win in the unspiked setting, while MNS dominates whenever spikes or structural change are present.

nodes.name: Minimum variance portfolio on DJIA tick data
nodes.statement: Given the simulation results described in the previous subsection, we next constructed a minimum variance portfolio using the three proposed NS estimators on intraday high-frequency data for the Dow Jones Industrial Average (DJIA). We collected tick-by-tick 30 DJIA stock prices from January 1, 2016 to December 31, 2016, comprising 252 trading days, from the Trade and Quote database.
nodes.statement_short: Out-of-sample minimum-variance portfolio built from 2016 tick-by-tick prices of the 30 DJIA constituents.

nodes.name: Minimum variance portfolio problem
nodes.statement: The minimum variance portfolio solves the following optimization problem \[ \min\limits_{\bw} \bw^{\mT} (\ICV) \bw, ~~\text{subject to}~\bw^{\mT}\bm{1}_p = 1, \] where $\bm{1}_p $ is a vector of $p$ ones and $\ICV$ is a given integrated covolatility matrix.
nodes.statement_short: Minimize $\bw^{\mT}(\ICV)\bw$ subject to $\bw^{\mT}\bm{1}_p=1$.

nodes.name: Minimum variance portfolio weights
nodes.statement: The solution of $\bw$ is \begin{equation} \bw = \frac{(\ICV)^{-1}\bm{1}_p}{\bm{1}_p^{\mT} (\ICV)^{-1}\bm{1}_p}. \end{equation}
nodes.statement_short: Closed-form weights $\bw=(\ICV)^{-1}\bm 1_p/(\bm 1_p^{\mT}(\ICV)^{-1}\bm 1_p)$.

nodes.name: Annualized return and standard deviation of the strategy
nodes.statement: For $\ell$-week training windows, $\hat\mu$ and $\hat\sigma$ are defined as \begin{equation} \hat\mu = \frac{252}{251 - \ell}\sum_{i = \ell + 1}^{251}\bw_i^{\mT}\bm r_i, ~ \hat{\sigma} = \left\{\frac{252}{251 - \ell}\sum_{i = \ell + 1}^{251}(\bw_i^{\mT}\bm r_i - \big(\frac{\hat\mu}{251 - \ell}\big)^2\right\}^{\frac{1}{2}}, \end{equation} where $\bw_i $ and $\bm r_i$ are the portfolio weights and returns, respectively, for the $i$th day.
nodes.statement_short: Annualized mean return and volatility of the daily rebalanced portfolio.

nodes.name: Empirical findings for the DJIA portfolios
nodes.statement: The ANS estimator had the smallest standard deviation and smallest maximum exposure for all settings. With 10-day training windows, the ANS estimator had the largest Sharpe ratio, but on average that of the MNS estimator was larger. Notably, the ANS and MNS estimators also had much lower computational costs compared with the NS estimator.
nodes.statement_short: ANS gives the lowest risk and exposure, MNS the best average Sharpe ratio, and both are far cheaper than NS.

nodes.name: Proof of Theorem 2.1
nodes.statement: Theorem \ref{thm:LSD_TVA} is a direct consequence of the following two propositions.
nodes.statement_short: Reduce Theorem 2.1 to Propositions A.1 and A.2.

nodes.name: Proposition A.1 (LSD of the self-normalized matrix $\wbSigma$)
nodes.statement: Under the assumptions of Theorem \ref{thm:LSD_TVA}, the ESD of $\wbSigma$, $F^{\wbSigma}$ converges almost surely to the limit $\widetilde{F}$, which is determined by $\breve{H}$ in that its Stieltjes transform $m_{\widetilde{F}}(z)$ satisfies the following equation: \begin{equation}m_{\widetilde{F}}(z) = \int_{\tau\in \mathbb{R}} \frac{1}{\tau(1 - \rho(1 + zm_{\widetilde{F}}(z))) - z}d\breve{H}(\tau),~\text{for}~z\in \mathbb{C}^+. \end{equation}
nodes.statement_short: The self-normalized matrix $\wbSigma$ and $\bbSigma$ are linked by the Marčenko–Pastur equation with ratio $\rho$.
conclusions: the ESD of $\wbSigma$, $F^{\wbSigma}$ converges almost surely to the limit $\widetilde{F}$, which is determined by $\breve{H}$ in that its Stieltjes transform $m_{\widetilde{F}}(z)$ satisfies the following equation: \begin{equation}m_{\widetilde{F}}(z) = \int_{\tau\in \mathbb{R}} \frac{1}{\tau(1 - \rho(1 + zm_{\widetilde{F}}(z))) - z}d\breve{H}(\tau),~\text{for}~z\in \mathbb{C}^+. \end{equation}

nodes.name: Proof of Proposition A.1
nodes.statement: Recall that \[\Delta\widebar{\bX}_{2i} = \sum_{j=1}^{L_{2i}}a_{2i,j}\Delta_{2i,j}\bX + \sum_{j=1}^{L_{2i-1}}b_{2i-1,j}\Delta_{2i-1,j}\bX,\] where $a_{i,j} = 1-\frac{j-1}{L_i}, b_{i,j} = \frac{j-1}{L_i}$, and $\Delta_{i,j}\bX = \bX_{T_{i-1}+j} - \bX_{T_{i-1}+j - 1}$. Then we separate $\Delta\widebar{\bX}_{2i}$ into two parts, \begin{equation} \Delta\wbX_{2i} = \sqrt{w_i}(\bLambda\bZ_{i} + \bV_i), \end{equation} where \begin{equation} w_i = \sum_{j=1}^{L_{2i}}a_{2i,j}^2\int_{s_{T_{2i-1} + j -1}}^{s_{T_{2i-1} + j}}\gamma_t^2dt + \sum_{j=1}^{L_{2i-1}}b_{2i-1,j}^2\int_{ s_{T_{2i-2} + j -1} }^{ s_{T_{2i-2} + j}}\gamma_t^2dt, \end{equation} \[\bZ_i = \frac{1}{\sqrt{w_i}}\left[\sum_{j=1}^{L_{2i}}a_{2i,j}\int_{s_{T_{2i-1} + j -1} }^{s_{T_{2i-1} + j} }\gamma_td\bW_t + \sum_{j=1}^{L_{2i-1}}b_{2i-1,j}\int_{s_{T_{2i-2} + j -1} }^{s_{T_{2i-2} + j} }\gamma_td\bW_t \right],\] and \[\bV_i = \frac{1}{\sqrt{w_i}}\left[\sum_{j=1}^{L_{2i}}a_{2i,j}\int_{s_{T_{2i-1} + j -1} }^{s_{T_{2i-1} + j} }\bmu_tdt + \sum_{j=1}^{L_{2i-1}}b_{2i-1,j}\int_{s_{T_{2i-2} + j -1} }^{s_{T_{2i-2} + j} }\bmu_tdt \right].\] Using the above notation, $\wbSigma$ can be rewritten as \[\wbSigma = \frac{p}{\hn}\sum_{i=1}^{\hn}\frac{\Delta\widebar{\bX}_{2i}\Delta\wbX_{2i}^{\mathrm{T}}}{|\Delta\wbX_{2i}|^2} = \frac{p}{\hn}\sum_{i=1}^\hn \frac{(\bV_i + \bLambda\bZ_i)(\bV_i + \bLambda\bZ_i)^{\mathrm{T}} }{|\bV_i + \bLambda\bZ_i|^2}.\] Notice that \[ \frac{1}{L_{2i}} \sum_{j = 1}^{L_{2i}} a_{2i,j} = \frac{1}{2}(1 + \frac{1}{L_{2i}}), ~~ \frac{1}{L_{2i - 1}}\sum_{j = 1}^{L_{2i - 1}} b_{2i-1, j} = \frac{1}{2}(1 - \frac{1}{L_{2i-1}}) \] and \[ \frac{1}{L_{2i}} \sum_{j = 1}^{L_{2i}} a_{2i,j}^2 = \frac{1}{3} + \frac{1}{6L_{2i}^2} + \frac{1}{2L_{2i}}, ~\frac{1}{L_{2i - 1}} \sum_{j = 1}^{L_{2i - 1}} b_{2i - 1,j}^2 = \frac{1}{3} + \frac{1}{6L_{2i - 1}^2} - \frac{1}{2L_{2i-1}}, \] which are all uniformly bounded as $L_i \geq 1$. By the boundedness of $|\mu_t^{(l)}|$ and $|\gamma_t|$ from Assumption \eqref{asm:bdd_mu} and \eqref{asm:bdd_gamma}, and the equally spaced transaction durations $\Delta s_{i,j}$ from Assumption \eqref{asm:bdd_duration}, there exists $C>0$ such that $|\bV_i^{(l)}|\leq C/\sqrt{\hn}$ for all $i=1,\cdots,\hn,l=1,\cdots, p$, which indicates that the $|\bV_i|$ are uniformly bounded. By a similar argument to that used in (3.34) in \cite{ZhengandLi20112}, we have \begin{equation} \max\limits_{1\leq i \leq \hn} \big|\frac{1}{p}|\bLambda\bZ_i|^2-1\big| \to 0, \hspace{0.5cm} \text{almost surely}. \end{equation} By the boundedness of the $|\bV_i|$, we further have \begin{equation} \max\limits_{1\leq i \leq \hn} \big|\frac{1}{p}|\bV_i + \bLambda\bZ_i|^2-1\big| \to 0, \hspace{0.5cm} \text{almost surely}. \end{equation} By the same arguments used in the proof of Theorem 2 in \cite{ZhengandLi20112}, we can show that Proposition \ref{prop: convergence of tilde sigma} holds.\proofend
nodes.statement_short: Split each averaged increment into $\sqrt{w_i}(\bLambda\bZ_i+\bV_i)$, show the drift part is negligible and $|\bLambda\bZ_i|^2/p\to1$, then quote Zheng and Li's argument.

nodes.name: Recall the triangular decomposition
nodes.statement: Recall that \[\Delta\widebar{\bX}_{2i} = \sum_{j=1}^{L_{2i}}a_{2i,j}\Delta_{2i,j}\bX + \sum_{j=1}^{L_{2i-1}}b_{2i-1,j}\Delta_{2i-1,j}\bX,\] where $a_{i,j} = 1-\frac{j-1}{L_i}, b_{i,j} = \frac{j-1}{L_i}$, and $\Delta_{i,j}\bX = \bX_{T_{i-1}+j} - \bX_{T_{i-1}+j - 1}$.
nodes.statement_short: Restate the asymmetric triangular form of the averaged increment.

nodes.name: Separate signal and drift
nodes.statement: Then we separate $\Delta\widebar{\bX}_{2i}$ into two parts, \begin{equation} \Delta\wbX_{2i} = \sqrt{w_i}(\bLambda\bZ_{i} + \bV_i), \end{equation} where \begin{equation} w_i = \sum_{j=1}^{L_{2i}}a_{2i,j}^2\int_{s_{T_{2i-1} + j -1}}^{s_{T_{2i-1} + j}}\gamma_t^2dt + \sum_{j=1}^{L_{2i-1}}b_{2i-1,j}^2\int_{ s_{T_{2i-2} + j -1} }^{ s_{T_{2i-2} + j}}\gamma_t^2dt, \end{equation} \[\bZ_i = \frac{1}{\sqrt{w_i}}\left[\sum_{j=1}^{L_{2i}}a_{2i,j}\int_{s_{T_{2i-1} + j -1} }^{s_{T_{2i-1} + j} }\gamma_td\bW_t + \sum_{j=1}^{L_{2i-1}}b_{2i-1,j}\int_{s_{T_{2i-2} + j -1} }^{s_{T_{2i-2} + j} }\gamma_td\bW_t \right],\] and \[\bV_i = \frac{1}{\sqrt{w_i}}\left[\sum_{j=1}^{L_{2i}}a_{2i,j}\int_{s_{T_{2i-1} + j -1} }^{s_{T_{2i-1} + j} }\bmu_tdt + \sum_{j=1}^{L_{2i-1}}b_{2i-1,j}\int_{s_{T_{2i-2} + j -1} }^{s_{T_{2i-2} + j} }\bmu_tdt \right].\]
nodes.statement_short: Write $\Delta\wbX_{2i}=\sqrt{w_i}(\bLambda\bZ_i+\bV_i)$ and define $w_i,\bZ_i,\bV_i$.

nodes.name: Rewrite $\wbSigma$ in the new variables
nodes.statement: Using the above notation, $\wbSigma$ can be rewritten as \[\wbSigma = \frac{p}{\hn}\sum_{i=1}^{\hn}\frac{\Delta\widebar{\bX}_{2i}\Delta\wbX_{2i}^{\mathrm{T}}}{|\Delta\wbX_{2i}|^2} = \frac{p}{\hn}\sum_{i=1}^\hn \frac{(\bV_i + \bLambda\bZ_i)(\bV_i + \bLambda\bZ_i)^{\mathrm{T}} }{|\bV_i + \bLambda\bZ_i|^2}.\]
nodes.statement_short: Express the self-normalized matrix in terms of $\bV_i+\bLambda\bZ_i$.

nodes.name: Bound the triangular weight sums
nodes.statement_short: The first and second moments of the weights $a_{i,j},b_{i,j}$ are uniformly bounded.

nodes.name: Bound the drift contribution
nodes.statement: By the boundedness of $|\mu_t^{(l)}|$ and $|\gamma_t|$ from Assumption \eqref{asm:bdd_mu} and \eqref{asm:bdd_gamma}, and the equally spaced transaction durations $\Delta s_{i,j}$ from Assumption \eqref{asm:bdd_duration}, there exists $C>0$ such that $|\bV_i^{(l)}|\leq C/\sqrt{\hn}$ for all $i=1,\cdots,\hn,l=1,\cdots, p$, which indicates that the $|\bV_i|$ are uniformly bounded.
nodes.statement_short: Assumptions (A.ii), (A.iii), (A.ix) give $|\bV_i^{(l)}|\leq C/\sqrt{N}$.

nodes.name: Concentration of $|\bLambda\bZ_i|^2/p$
nodes.statement: By a similar argument to that used in (3.34) in \cite{ZhengandLi20112}, we have \begin{equation} \max\limits_{1\leq i \leq \hn} \big|\frac{1}{p}|\bLambda\bZ_i|^2-1\big| \to 0, \hspace{0.5cm} \text{almost surely}. \end{equation}
nodes.statement_short: Import Zheng and Li's estimate that $|\bLambda\bZ_i|^2/p\to1$ uniformly.

nodes.name: Transfer the concentration to $\bV_i+\bLambda\bZ_i$
nodes.statement: By the boundedness of the $|\bV_i|$, we further have \begin{equation} \max\limits_{1\leq i \leq \hn} \big|\frac{1}{p}|\bV_i + \bLambda\bZ_i|^2-1\big| \to 0, \hspace{0.5cm} \text{almost surely}. \end{equation}
nodes.statement_short: The same normalization holds after adding the drift term.

nodes.name: Conclude by the cited argument
nodes.statement: By the same arguments used in the proof of Theorem 2 in \cite{ZhengandLi20112}, we can show that Proposition \ref{prop: convergence of tilde sigma} holds.\proofend
nodes.statement_short: Conclude Proposition A.1 exactly as in Zheng and Li's Theorem 2.

nodes.name: Proposition A.2 (limit of the ICV spectrum and of the normalizing sum)
nodes.statement: Under the assumptions of Theorem \ref{thm:LSD_TVA}, the ESD of the ICV matrix converges almost surely in distribution to a probability distribution $H$ as $p\to\infty$ defined by \begin{equation} H(x) = \breve{H}(x/\theta), \end{equation} where $\theta = \int_0^1(\gamma_t^*)^2dt$. Moreover, \begin{equation} \lim\limits_{p\to\infty} \frac{1}{p}\sum_{i = 1}^N |\Delta\wbX_{2i}|^2 = \int_0^1 (\dfrac 13 + \dfrac 16 f_{2,s}^*)(\gamma_s^*)^2ds,\hspace{0.5cm} \text{almost surely}. \end{equation}
nodes.statement_short: The ICV spectrum converges to $H(x)=\breve H(x/\theta)$ and $p^{-1}\sum|\Delta\wbX_{2i}|^2$ converges to $\int_0^1(1/3+f_{2,s}^*/6)(\gamma_s^*)^2ds$.
conclusions: the ESD of the ICV matrix converges almost surely in distribution to a probability distribution $H$ as $p\to\infty$ defined by \begin{equation} H(x) = \breve{H}(x/\theta), \end{equation} where $\theta = \int_0^1(\gamma_t^*)^2dt$.

nodes.name: Proof of Proposition A.2
nodes.statement:
The convergence of $F^{ICV}$ follows from Assumption \eqref{asm:LSD_bH} and the fact that \[F^{\ICV}(x) = F^{ reve{ Sigma}}\left( rac{x}{\int_0^1\gamma_t^2dt}ight) \hspace{0.5cm} 	ext{for all~} x\geq 0.\] We proceed to show the convergence of $1/p\cdot \sum_{i=1}^N|\Delta \wbX_{2i}|^2$. Write $\Delta \wbX_{2i} = \sqrt{w_i}( Lambda  Z_i +  V_i)$ as in \eqref{eq: expression of delta wbx}; then \[ \dfrac 1p |\Delta\wbX_{2i}|^2 = \dfrac 1p \sum_{i=1}^N w_i | V_i +  Lambda  Z_i|^2 =\sum_{i=1}^N Ew_i + \sum_{i=1}^N (w_i - Ew_i) + \varepsilon, \] where $\varepsilon = \sum_{i = 1}^N w_i (p^{-1} | V_i +  Lambda  Z_i|^2 - 1)$. Besides, $\sum_{i=1}^N (w_i - E(w_i))$ converges to zero almost surely by the Kolmogorov strong law of large numbers and the boundedness of $\max\limits_{i,n} (N w_i)$. Next, we show that there exists a piecewise continuous process $(w_s)$ with finite jumps such that \[ \lim_{n	o\infty}\sum_{i=1}^N \int_{(2i-2)/n}^{2i/n}|N E(w_i) - w_s|ds =0, \] where $w_s = (\dfrac 13 + \dfrac 16 f_{2,s}^*)\cdot (\gamma_s^*)^2$. Suppose that $(\gamma_t^*)$, $(f_{1,s}^*)$, and $(f_{2,s}^*)$ have a finite number of jumps J in total. For each $j = 1,\cdots, J$, there exists an $\ell_j$ such that the $j$th jump falls in the interval $((2\ell_j - 2)/n, 2\ell_j/n]$. Then  egin{equation*}  egin{split} &\sum_{i=1}^\hn\int_{(2i-2)/n}^{2i/n}|N E(w_i) - w_s|ds\ =&\sum\limits_{\ell_j \in \{\ell_1,\cdots,\ell_J\}}\int_{ rac{2\ell_j-2}{n}}^{ rac{2\ell_j}{n}}|N E(w_{\ell_j}) - w_s|ds + \sum\limits_{i 
otin \{\ell_1,\cdots,\ell_J\}}\int_{ rac{2i-2}{n}}^{ rac{2i}{n}}|N E(w_i) - w_s|ds\ := &D_1 + D_2.\ \end{split} \end{equation*} As $(N w_{\ell_j})$, $|\gamma_s^*|$, and $|f_{2,s}^*|$ are bounded, for any $\epsilon >0$ and for sufficiently large $n$, we have \[|D_1|\leq  rac{2}{n}JC <\epsilon.\] Notice that \[ E \left( rac{1}{L_{2i}}\sum_{j = 1}^{L_{2i}}a_{2i,j}^2 ight)=  rac{1}{3} +  rac{1}{6}E ig( rac{1}{L_{2i}^2} ig) +  rac{1}{2}E ig( rac{1}{L_{2i}} ig), \] and \[ E\left(  rac{1}{L_{2i-1}}\sum_{j = 1}^{L_{2i-1}}b_{2i-1 ,j}^2 ight) =  rac{1}{3} +  rac{1}{6} E ig(  rac{1}{L_{2i-1}^2} ig) -  rac{1}{2} E ig(  rac{1}{L_{2i-1}} ig). \] For the second term $D_2$, because $(\gamma_t^*)$, $f_{1,s}^*$, and $f_{2,s}^*$ are continuous in $[(2i-2)/n, 2i/n]$ when $i 
otin \{\ell_1,\cdots,\ell_J\}$, and by Assumption \eqref{asm:bdd_ICV} and \eqref{asm:moment_L}, $(\gamma_t)$, $(f_{1,s})$, and $(f_{2,s})$ uniformly converge to $(\gamma_t^*)$, $(f_{1,s}^*)$, and $(f_{2,s}^*)$, respectively. For any $\epsilon >0$ and for sufficiently large $n,p$, we have \[|\gamma_t^* - \gamma_{2i/n}|<\epsilon, ~~ 	ext{and}~~ |f_{2, 2i/n}^* - f_{2, t}^*|<\epsilon, ~~ 	ext{for all} ~~t \in [ rac{2i-2}{n}, rac{2i}{n} ],\] for $i = 1,\cdots, N$ and $|\gamma_t - \gamma_t^*|<\epsilon$ for all $t\in [0,1]$. Define \[  egin{split} w_i^* &= \sum_{j=1}^{L_{2i}}a_{2i,j}^2\int_{s_{T_{2i-1} + j -1}}^{s_{T_{2i-1} + j}}(\gamma_t^*)^2dt + \sum_{j=1}^{L_{2i-1}}b_{2i-1,j}^2\int_{ s_{T_{2i-2} + j -1} }^{ s_{T_{2i-2} + j}}(\gamma_t^*)^2dt,\ 	w_i^*&= (\gamma_{2i/n}^*)^2  rac{1}{nL_{2i}}\sum_{j=1}^{L_{2i}}a_{2i,j}^2 + (\gamma_{2i/n}^*)^2  rac{1}{nL_{2i-1}}\sum_{j=1}^{L_{2i-1}}b_{2i-1,j}^2\ 	ext{and}~~~ 	tw_i^*&=(\gamma_{2i/n}^*)^2\cdot rac{2}{n} igg( rac{1}{3} +  rac{1}{6}f_{2, 2i/n}^* igg). \end{split} \] For all large $n$, because $|\gamma_t|\leq C$ and $1\leq L_i< L^*$, for any $i, t$, we have \[  egin{split} &|D_2| \ \leq& \sum\limits_{i}\int_{ rac{2i-2}{n}}^{ rac{2i}{n}}N|E(w_i) - E(w_i^*)|ds + \sum\limits_{i

otin \{\ell_1,\cdots,\ell_J\}}\int_{ rac{2i-2}{n}}^{ rac{2i}{n}}| N	tw_i^* - w_s|ds\ 	o& 0, ~~~	ext{almost surely.} \end{split} \] This completes the proof of \eqref{eq: convergence of Vi plus lambda Zi}.\proofend
nodes.statement_short: Rescale the ESD of $\bbSigma$, then split $\sum w_i$ into its mean, a strong-law fluctuation and an error term, and control the mean by a jump/continuity decomposition $D_1+D_2$.

nodes.name: Rescaling of the ICV spectrum
nodes.statement: The convergence of $F^{ICV}$ follows from Assumption \eqref{asm:LSD_bH} and the fact that \[F^{\ICV}(x) = F^{\breve{\bSigma}}\left(\frac{x}{\int_0^1\gamma_t^2dt}\right) \hspace{0.5cm} \text{for all~} x\geq 0.\]
nodes.statement_short: $F^{\ICV}$ is a rescaling of $F^{\breve\bSigma}$, so Assumption (A.vii) gives its limit.

nodes.name: Decompose the normalizing sum
nodes.statement: We proceed to show the convergence of $1/p\cdot \sum_{i=1}^N|\Delta \wbX_{2i}|^2$. Write $\Delta \wbX_{2i} = \sqrt{w_i}(\bLambda \bZ_i + \bV_i)$ as in \eqref{eq: expression of delta wbx}; then \[ \dfrac 1p |\Delta\wbX_{2i}|^2 = \dfrac 1p \sum_{i=1}^N w_i |\bV_i + \bLambda \bZ_i|^2 =\sum_{i=1}^N Ew_i + \sum_{i=1}^N (w_i - Ew_i) + \varepsilon, \] where $\varepsilon = \sum_{i = 1}^N w_i (p^{-1} |\bV_i + \bLambda \bZ_i|^2 - 1)$.
nodes.statement_short: Split $p^{-1}\sum|\Delta\wbX_{2i}|^2$ into $\sum Ew_i$, a centred sum, and an error $\varepsilon$.

nodes.name: The error term vanishes
nodes.statement: First, almost surely, that $\max\limits_{i,n} (N w_i)$ is bounded follows from Assumption \eqref{asm:bdd_gamma} and \eqref{asm:bdd_duration}. Thus, combining this with the convergence of \eqref{eq: order of v pluz z}, the error term $\varepsilon$ converges to 0 almost surely.
nodes.statement_short: Boundedness of $Nw_i$ plus the earlier normalization kills $\varepsilon$.

nodes.name: The centred sum vanishes
nodes.statement: Besides, $\sum_{i=1}^N (w_i - E(w_i))$ converges to zero almost surely by the Kolmogorov strong law of large numbers and the boundedness of $\max\limits_{i,n} (N w_i)$.
nodes.statement_short: Apply Kolmogorov's strong law to the centred weights.

nodes.name: Target a piecewise continuous limit process
nodes.statement: Next, we show that there exists a piecewise continuous process $(w_s)$ with finite jumps such that \[ \lim_{n\to\infty}\sum_{i=1}^N \int_{(2i-2)/n}^{2i/n}|N E(w_i) - w_s|ds =0, \] where $w_s = (\dfrac 13 + \dfrac 16 f_{2,s}^*)\cdot (\gamma_s^*)^2$.
nodes.statement_short: Reduce to an $L^1$ approximation of $NE(w_i)$ by $w_s=(1/3+f_{2,s}^*/6)(\gamma_s^*)^2$.

nodes.name: Split over jump and continuity intervals
nodes.statement: Suppose that $(\gamma_t^*)$, $(f_{1,s}^*)$, and $(f_{2,s}^*)$ have a finite number of jumps J in total. For each $j = 1,\cdots, J$, there exists an $\ell_j$ such that the $j$th jump falls in the interval $((2\ell_j - 2)/n, 2\ell_j/n]$. Then \begin{equation*} \begin{split} &\sum_{i=1}^\hn\int_{(2i-2)/n}^{2i/n}|N E(w_i) - w_s|ds\\ =&\sum\limits_{\ell_j \in \{\ell_1,\cdots,\ell_J\}}\int_{\frac{2\ell_j-2}{n}}^{\frac{2\ell_j}{n}}|N E(w_{\ell_j}) - w_s|ds + \sum\limits_{i \notin \{\ell_1,\cdots,\ell_J\}}\int_{\frac{2i-2}{n}}^{\frac{2i}{n}}|N E(w_i) - w_s|ds\\ := &D_1 + D_2.\\ \end{split} \end{equation*}
nodes.statement_short: Separate the finitely many jump intervals ($D_1$) from the continuity intervals ($D_2$).

nodes.name: Bound the jump part $D_1$
nodes.statement: As $(N w_{\ell_j})$, $|\gamma_s^*|$, and $|f_{2,s}^*|$ are bounded, for any $\epsilon >0$ and for sufficiently large $n$, we have \[|D_1|\leq \frac{2}{n}JC <\epsilon.\]
nodes.statement_short: Only $J$ intervals of length $2/n$ contribute, so $D_1=O(J/n)$.

nodes.name: Moment identities for the triangular weights
nodes.statement: Notice that \[ E \left(\frac{1}{L_{2i}}\sum_{j = 1}^{L_{2i}}a_{2i,j}^2 \right)= \frac{1}{3} + \frac{1}{6}E\big(\frac{1}{L_{2i}^2}\big) + \frac{1}{2}E\big(\frac{1}{L_{2i}}\big), \] and \[ E\left( \frac{1}{L_{2i-1}}\sum_{j = 1}^{L_{2i-1}}b_{2i-1 ,j}^2 \right) = \frac{1}{3} + \frac{1}{6} E\big( \frac{1}{L_{2i-1}^2}\big) - \frac{1}{2} E\big( \frac{1}{L_{2i-1}}\big). \]
nodes.statement_short: Take expectations of the weight sums, producing $1/3+E(L^{-2})/6\pm E(L^{-1})/2$.

nodes.name: Bound the continuity part $D_2$ and conclude
nodes.statement:
For the second term $D_2$, because $(\gamma_t^*)$, $f_{1,s}^*$, and $f_{2,s}^*$ are continuous in $[(2i-2)/n, 2i/n]$ when $i 
otin \{\ell_1,\cdots,\ell_J\}$, and by Assumption \eqref{asm:bdd_ICV} and \eqref{asm:moment_L}, $(\gamma_t)$, $(f_{1,s})$, and $(f_{2,s})$ uniformly converge to $(\gamma_t^*)$, $(f_{1,s}^*)$, and $(f_{2,s}^*)$, respectively. For any $\epsilon >0$ and for sufficiently large $n,p$, we have \[|\gamma_t^* - \gamma_{2i/n}|<\epsilon, ~~ 	ext{and}~~ |f_{2, 2i/n}^* - f_{2, t}^*|<\epsilon, ~~ 	ext{for all} ~~t \in [ rac{2i-2}{n}, rac{2i}{n} ],\] for $i = 1,\cdots, N$ and $|\gamma_t - \gamma_t^*|<\epsilon$ for all $t\in [0,1]$. Define \[  egin{split} w_i^* &= \sum_{j=1}^{L_{2i}}a_{2i,j}^2\int_{s_{T_{2i-1} + j -1}}^{s_{T_{2i-1} + j}}(\gamma_t^*)^2dt + \sum_{j=1}^{L_{2i-1}}b_{2i-1,j}^2\int_{ s_{T_{2i-2} + j -1} }^{ s_{T_{2i-2} + j}}(\gamma_t^*)^2dt,\ 	w_i^*&= (\gamma_{2i/n}^*)^2  rac{1}{nL_{2i}}\sum_{j=1}^{L_{2i}}a_{2i,j}^2 + (\gamma_{2i/n}^*)^2  rac{1}{nL_{2i-1}}\sum_{j=1}^{L_{2i-1}}b_{2i-1,j}^2\ 	ext{and}~~~ 	tw_i^*&=(\gamma_{2i/n}^*)^2\cdot rac{2}{n} igg( rac{1}{3} +  rac{1}{6}f_{2, 2i/n}^* igg). \end{split} \] For all large $n$, because $|\gamma_t|\leq C$ and $1\leq L_i< L^*$, for any $i, t$, we have \[  egin{split} &|D_2| \ \leq& \sum\limits_{i}\int_{ rac{2i-2}{n}}^{ rac{2i}{n}}N|E(w_i) - E(w_i^*)|ds + \sum\limits_{i
otin \{\ell_1,\cdots,\ell_J\}}\int_{ rac{2i-2}{n}}^{ rac{2i}{n}}N| E(w_i^*) - E(	w_i^*)|ds \ +&\sum\limits_{i}\int_{ rac{2i-2}{n}}^{ rac{2i}{n}}| NE(	w_i^*) - N	tw_i^*|ds +\sum\limits_{i
otin \{\ell_1,\cdots,\ell_J\}}\int_{ rac{2i-2}{n}}^{ rac{2i}{n}}| N	tw_i^* - w_s|ds\ 	o& 0, ~~~	ext{almost surely.} \end{split} \] This completes the proof of \eqref{eq: convergence of Vi plus lambda Zi}.\proofend
nodes.statement_short: Chain four comparisons $w_i\to w_i^*\to\tw_i^*\to\ttw_i^*\to w_s$ using uniform convergence.

nodes.name: Proof of Theorem 2.2
nodes.statement: The convergence of the ESD of the ICV was proved in Theorem \ref{thm:LSD_TVA}. The rest of Theorem \ref{thm: theorem for the TVAPA} is a direct consequence of the following two lemmas.
nodes.statement_short: Reduce Theorem 2.2 to Lemmas B.1 and B.2, the ICV part being already proved.

nodes.name: Lemma B.1 (LSD of the pre-averaged self-normalized matrix)
nodes.statement: Under the assumptions of Theorem \ref{thm: theorem for the TVAPA}, the ESD of $\hbSigma$ converges almost surely, and the limit $F^{\hbSigma}$ is determined by $\breve{H}$ in that its Stieltjes transform $m_{\hbSigma}(z)$ satisfies the following equation: \begin{equation}m_{\hbSigma}(z) = \int_{\tau\in \mathbb{R}} \frac{1}{\tau(1 - c(1 + zm_{\hbSigma}(z))) - z}d\breve{H}(\tau),\hspace{0.2cm}\text{for}~z\in \mathbb{C^+}. \end{equation}
nodes.statement_short: $\hbSigma$ has a limiting spectral distribution determined by $\breve H$ through the Marčenko–Pastur equation with ratio $c$.
assumptions: Under the assumptions of Theorem \ref{thm: theorem for the TVAPA}
conclusions: the ESD of $\hbSigma$ converges almost surely, and the limit $F^{\hbSigma}$ is determined by $\breve{H}$ in that its Stieltjes transform $m_{\hbSigma}(z)$ satisfies the following equation: \begin{equation}m_{\hbSigma}(z) = \int_{\tau\in \mathbb{R}} \frac{1}{\tau(1 - c(1 + zm_{\hbSigma}(z))) - z}d\breve{H}(\tau),\hspace{0.2cm}\text{for}~z\in \mathbb{C^+}. \end{equation}

nodes.name: Lemma B.2 (consistency of the scale estimator $\hat\theta_p$)
nodes.statement: Under the assumptions of Theorem \ref{thm: theorem for the TVAPA}, we have \begin{equation}\lim_{p\to\infty}3\frac{\sum_{i=1}^\hv|\Delta\wwbY_{2i}|^2}{p} = \theta, \hspace{0.5cm}\text{almost surely}. \end{equation}
nodes.statement_short: Three times the normalized sum of squared pre-averaged noisy returns converges to $\theta$.
assumptions: Under the assumptions of Theorem \ref{thm: theorem for the TVAPA}

nodes.statement:
To prove the convergence of $F^{\hbSigma}$, we shall show that \[ \hbSigma =  rac{p}{\hv} \sum_{i=1}^\hv rac{\Delta	wbY_{2i}(\Delta	wbY_{2i})^{\mathrm{T}}}{|\Delta	wbY_{2i}|^2}~~~	ext{and}~~~ 	tbSigma :=  rac{p}{\hv}\sum_{i=1}^{\hv} rac{\Delta	wbX_{2i}\Delta	wbX_{2i}^{\mathrm{T}}}{|\Delta	wbX_{2i}|^2} \] have the same LSD. Following the same arguments as in the proof of Proposition C.1 of \cite{XiaandZheng20182}, it suffices to show that  egin{equation} \max\limits_{1\leq i \leq \hv, 1\leq j \leq p}  rac{\sqrt{p}|\Delta	wbe_{2i}^{(j)}|}{|\Delta	wbX_{2i}|}	o 0,\hspace{1cm} 	ext{almost surely}. \end{equation} We start by showing that there exists a constant $\widetilde{C}>0$ for large $M$, such that  egin{equation} \min\limits_{1\leq i \leq M} |\Delta	wbX_{2i}|^2 \geq \widetilde{C}. \end{equation} By equation \eqref{eqn:Delta_V}, we decompose $\Delta	wbX_{2i}$ as follows:  egin{align*} \Delta	wbX_{2i}= &  rac{1}{h}\sum_{j=1}^{h}\left(\wbX_{(2i-1)h + j} - \wbX_{(2i-2)h}ight) -  rac{1}{h}\sum_{j=1}^{h}\left( \wbX_{(2i-2)h+j} - \wbX_{(2i-2)h}ight)

otag\ &+ \sum_{l=1}^{2h-1}\sum_{j=1}^{L_{(2i-2)h + l}} \left(1- rac{|h-l+1|}{h}ight)\Delta_{(2i-2)h+l,j} X
